questions.question: How does a select statement choose among channel operations in Go?
questions.title: How Go select chooses a ready case
questions.direct_answer: A select evaluates its channel operands and send values once on entry, then considers which communications can proceed. If exactly one is ready, that case runs. If several are ready, one is chosen using a uniform pseudo-random selection; source order is not priority. If none is ready, select runs default when present or blocks until a communication becomes ready.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner knows exact readiness, evaluation, blocking, and multiple-ready selection rules.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: select works with channel send and receive cases.
Channel operands and send values are evaluated once on entry.
Several ready communications are chosen uniformly pseudo-randomly.
With none ready, default runs or the select blocks.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A `select` coordinates several possible channel communications. Each case is a send or receive, with at most one `default`. It is not a general Boolean switch; readiness of the channel operation determines which case can run.

On entering select, Go evaluates the channel operands and values for send cases once, in source order. It then builds the set of communications that can proceed immediately. A buffered receive is ready when a value is available, an unbuffered operation is ready when its matching peer is ready, and a receive from a closed channel is ready.

If one case can proceed, Go chooses it. If several can proceed, one is selected uniformly pseudo-randomly. The first textual case has no priority, so correctness must not depend on a cancellation case always winning over a simultaneously ready data case.

For example, two buffered channels can each contain a value before select begins. Either receive case may run first. The program can accept either result, then read the other channel separately if it needs both values.

If no communication can proceed and there is no default, select blocks until something becomes ready. With a default, it executes immediately instead. I use select for competing communications, cancellation, or timeouts, and design every case so any permitted choice preserves the program's invariant. Tests should accept every valid ready-case ordering rather than encode a false priority.

sections.title: Readiness is the decision input
sections.content: A select does not poll cases from top to bottom. It forms a ready set from channel operations, chooses one eligible communication, performs it, and executes that case body. Blocking or default applies only when the ready set is empty.

sections.title: Walk through the five selection steps
sections.content:
First, all channel expressions in receive cases and the channel and right-hand-side expressions in send cases are evaluated once, following source order. Side effects in those expressions occur even when their case is not eventually selected, so complicated expressions make the behavior harder to review.

Second, the runtime determines which communications can proceed. A receive can use an available buffered value, pair with a sender, or observe a closed channel. A send can use free buffer space or pair with a receiver. An operation on a nil channel can never proceed and is absent from the ready set.

Third, if the set contains at least one operation, exactly one is chosen. With several, the language specifies a uniform pseudo-random choice. This avoids a source-order priority promise, but it is not a scheduling fairness guarantee for an entire long-running system.

Fourth, the chosen communication completes, and any receive assignment is applied. Fifth, statements in that case execute. If the ready set was empty, default executes when present; otherwise the goroutine waits until a case can proceed and repeats the selection decision.

Design follows from those rules. A case should leave state valid even when another simultaneously ready case was not chosen. If cancellation must prevent processing after a particular boundary, check that boundary explicitly rather than treating the first case as privileged. Keep case bodies short so the goroutine can return to coordination promptly.

sections.title: The select decision
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Evaluate channel operands once] --> B[Build ready communication set]
  B --> C{How many ready?}
  C -- One --> D[Perform that communication]
  C -- Several --> E[Uniform pseudo-random choice]
  E --> D
  C -- None, default exists --> F[Run default]
  C -- None, no default --> G[Block until ready]
  G --> B
```

questions.question: How do nil and closed channels behave inside select?
questions.title: Nil and closed channels in select
questions.direct_answer: A send or receive on a nil channel can never proceed, so assigning nil dynamically disables that select case. A receive from a closed channel is always ready: it yields buffered values first, then the element type's zero value with ok false. Sending on a closed channel panics. These rules make nil useful for state-driven case control and require closed receives to test ok or be disabled.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner can reason about disabled nil cases, closed receive readiness, and safe loop control.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A nil channel send or receive never becomes ready.
Setting a channel variable to nil disables its select case.
A closed channel yields buffered values before zero values.
After draining, receive returns the zero value and ok false immediately.
Sending on a closed channel panics.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Nil and closed channels have opposite readiness behavior. Communication on a nil channel blocks forever, so a nil send or receive case can never enter the ready set of a select. Code can assign a channel variable to nil to turn that case off without rebuilding the select.

A closed channel behaves differently for receivers. Any buffered values are received normally with `ok` true. After the buffer is empty, receives complete immediately with the element type's zero value and `ok` false. That makes a closed receive case continuously ready.

In a loop, failing to inspect `ok` can process endless zero values or make the closed case dominate future selections. The usual pattern handles closure and sets the local channel variable to nil, disabling that case while other inputs remain active.

For example, the runnable code has one closed buffered channel and one nil channel. Select cannot choose the nil case. It first receives the buffered seven with `ok` true; the next direct receive gets zero with `ok` false because the closed buffer is drained.

Channel closing also has ownership rules. Sending on a closed channel panics, as does closing an already closed channel. I let the sending owner close a data channel after its final send, and I use nil only on a local channel variable that controls this goroutine's selection state.

sections.title: Nil disables; close broadcasts readiness
sections.content: Nil means there is no communication endpoint yet, so the operation cannot proceed. Close means no future values will be sent, so receivers can finish immediately. Select uses those language rules directly when it constructs its ready set.

sections.title: Concept guide · Nil and closed channels in select
sections.content:
A channel variable contains either a channel value or nil. Send and receive operations on nil block forever. Inside select they therefore contribute no ready case. This is useful when an output should be enabled only while a queued value exists or an input should be disabled after completion.

Closing does not erase buffered values. Receivers drain them in order with `ok` true. Once empty, every receive can proceed immediately and returns the zero value with `ok` false. A `for range` loop stops at that boundary automatically, while an explicit select receive must usually inspect the Boolean.

Consider merging two inputs. When the first closes, set its local variable to nil. The select continues listening to the second input rather than repeatedly choosing the permanently ready closed channel. When both variables are nil, no communication can proceed; the surrounding loop must terminate instead of entering a select that blocks forever.

A send to a closed channel is a programming error and panics. Only code that owns the sending lifecycle should close a data channel, after all senders are finished. Receivers normally observe closure; they do not close a channel merely because they no longer want values. Cancellation needs a separate signal or context when producers must stop early.

These rules are deterministic even though multi-ready choice is not. Nil is never ready. A drained closed receive is always ready. Bugs come from applying the wrong lifecycle meaning: nil is disabled, close is a broadcast that sending is finished, and neither is a general-purpose reset operation.

sections.title: Channel state and readiness
sections.content:
| Channel operation | Can select choose it? | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Receive from nil | No | Disabled forever while nil |
| Send to nil | No | Disabled forever while nil |
| Receive buffered value from closed channel | Yes | Value, `ok == true` |
| Receive from drained closed channel | Yes | Zero value, `ok == false` |
| Send to closed channel | Panics if executed | Programming error |

sections.title: Observe buffered, closed, and nil behavior
sections.content:
```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	values := make(chan int, 1)
	values <- 7
	close(values)

	var disabled <-chan int
	select {
	case <-disabled:
		panic("nil channel became ready")
	case value, ok := <-values:
		fmt.Println(value, ok)
	}

	value, ok := <-values
	fmt.Println(value, ok)
}
```
The output is `7 true` followed by `0 false`. The nil case is disabled and cannot be selected.

questions.question: What does default do in select, and when can it cause a busy loop?
questions.title: Non-blocking select and busy-loop risk
questions.direct_answer: A default case runs immediately when no channel communication is ready, making select non-blocking. This is useful for a deliberate try-send or try-receive that reports failure to proceed. Repeating such a select in a loop without blocking, waiting, or useful bounded work can consume CPU and starve other behavior. For ordinary waiting, omit default and add explicit cancellation or timer cases instead.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner can distinguish a one-shot non-blocking operation from an accidental polling loop.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: default runs only when no communication case is ready.
Its presence makes that select non-blocking.
Use it for explicit try-send or try-receive semantics.
A loop that repeatedly reaches default can spin at full CPU.
Omit default when the goroutine should wait for work or cancellation.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
In a select, `default` is chosen only when none of the channel communications can proceed immediately. Because the goroutine does not wait, the select becomes a non-blocking attempt rather than a normal blocking coordination point.

That behavior is useful when failure to communicate is an expected result. A `trySend` helper can return false when a bounded queue is full, and a metrics path can intentionally drop or count that event. A `tryReceive` can check whether a cached notification is already available.

The same default is dangerous inside an unbounded loop. If no channel is ready, the goroutine can execute default and return to select millions of times, consuming a CPU core. Adding `runtime.Gosched` or a tiny sleep hides the polling design rather than expressing when work should resume.

For example, the code uses a one-slot channel. The first try-send succeeds and the second returns false immediately because the buffer is full. After receiving the first value, a later send could succeed. No polling loop is needed.

When a worker should wait, I omit default and include the actual events: work, `ctx.Done()`, or a timer channel. I use default only when the API is explicitly non-blocking and the caller has a meaningful plan for the not-ready result, such as backpressure, dropping, or doing independent bounded work.

sections.title: Default changes the waiting contract
sections.content: Without default, select is a suspension point until communication can proceed. With default, it is an immediate readiness test. That small syntactic change should match an explicit product decision about backpressure, dropping, or alternative work.

sections.title: Design the not-ready path deliberately
sections.content:
Start with the caller's requirement. If a value must eventually be delivered, a blocking send with cancellation is usually correct. If the system may reject work when a bounded queue is full, a non-blocking send can return a Boolean or error. The caller then owns retry, drop, or fallback policy.

Default is evaluated only after Go determines that no communication case can proceed. It has no priority over a ready channel. In a one-shot helper this produces a clear try-operation: success means the communication happened, false means it did not happen at that instant.

Trouble begins when the not-ready branch immediately repeats. The loop has no event that parks the goroutine, so it becomes active polling. It may waste CPU, distort scheduler behavior, and make tests appear timing-dependent. A sleep introduces latency and tuning rather than restoring event-driven coordination.

Replace the loop with the event that should wake it. A worker can block on jobs and context cancellation. Periodic work can include a `time.Ticker` case. A deadline can use Context or a timer. If useful computation exists between attempts, bound that computation and re-evaluate whether queue rejection is still the intended contract.

Backpressure is the deeper design decision. A blocking send slows producers to match consumers. A bounded non-blocking send rejects overflow. An unbounded queue moves the limit into memory. Default is appropriate only for the second design; it should not be added merely to make a blocked goroutine appear responsive.

sections.title: One-shot try operation versus accidental polling
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Enter select] --> B{Communication ready?}
  B -- Yes --> C[Perform send or receive]
  B -- No, default --> D[Return not-ready result]
  D --> E{Caller has explicit policy?}
  E -- Drop, retry later, other bounded work --> F[Valid non-blocking design]
  E -- Immediately loop --> G[Busy loop and CPU waste]
```
